name: Cyclical mastalgia
rawContent:
# Cyclical Mastalgia: Comprehensive Reference for Foundation Year Doctors

## 1. OVERVIEW

### Definition and Key Concepts
Cyclical mastalgia (also called cyclical breast pain or cyclical mastodynia) is breast pain that varies with the menstrual cycle, typically worsening in the luteal phase (1-2 weeks before menstruation) and improving with the onset of menses. It is a benign condition and one of the most common breast symptoms, accounting for ~70% of breast pain presentations.

### Epidemiology
Extremely common—affects up to 70% of women at some point during reproductive years. Peak incidence is in the third and fourth decades (25-45 years). Severe cyclical mastalgia requiring treatment occurs in ~10-20% of women. Rare after menopause unless on hormone replacement therapy (HRT).

### Essential Pathophysiology
The exact mechanism is unclear but thought to be multifactorial:
- **Hormonal influence**: Fluctuating estrogen and progesterone levels during the menstrual cycle cause breast tissue changes (proliferation, edema, increased ductal activity)
- **Increased water retention** in breast tissue during the luteal phase
- **Prolactin sensitivity**: Some studies suggest abnormal prolactin response
- **Essential fatty acid imbalance**: Deficiency in gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) may increase breast tissue sensitivity to circulating hormones
- **Caffeine/methylxanthines**: May exacerbate symptoms by increasing cyclic AMP levels
- **Breast tissue composition**: Women with dense, nodular breast tissue more prone to pain

Cyclical mastalgia is NOT associated with increased breast cancer risk.

## 2. RECOGNITION

### Key Symptoms
- Bilateral breast pain or discomfort (though may be unilateral or asymmetric)
- Pain typically affects **upper outer quadrants** of breasts
- **Cyclical pattern**: Worsens 1-2 weeks before menstruation (luteal phase), relieves with onset of period
- Described as heaviness, dull ache, tenderness, or soreness
- Breast swelling or lumpiness (diffuse nodularity, not discrete lump)
- May radiate to axilla or upper arm
- Pain severity varies cycle to cycle
- Interferes with daily activities, sleep, or sexual activity in severe cases

### Key Signs
- Bilateral breast tenderness on palpation (especially upper outer quadrants)
- **Diffuse nodularity** ("lumpy" texture throughout)—benign fibrocystic change
- No discrete dominant mass
- No skin changes (no erythema, peau d'orange, nipple retraction)
- No nipple discharge (or may have clear/milky bilateral discharge—physiological)
- No axillary lymphadenopathy
- Examination findings vary with menstrual cycle (less nodularity after menstruation)

### Atypical Presentations
- Predominantly unilateral pain (20-30% of cases)
- Severe pain requiring analgesia
- Pain persisting into menstruation (though should improve)
- First presentation in perimenopause
- Pain associated with oral contraceptive pill (OCP) or HRT use

### Red Flags Requiring Immediate Action
- **Discrete, hard, fixed lump** (possible malignancy)
- **Unilateral spontaneous bloody nipple discharge** (possible intraductal papilloma or malignancy)
- **Skin changes**: erythema, peau d'orange, ulceration, nipple retraction/inversion (inflammatory breast cancer or locally advanced cancer)
- **Axillary lymphadenopathy** (possible malignancy)
- **Unilateral persistent pain** in postmenopausal woman (higher cancer risk)
- **Persistent localized pain** unrelated to menstrual cycle (non-cyclical mastalgia—different etiology, requires investigation)
- **Systemic symptoms**: weight loss, night sweats (malignancy)
- **Age >40 with new symptoms** (urgent 2-week wait referral if red flags present)

## 3. INVESTIGATION

### First-line Investigations
- **Clinical history**: Detailed pain diary (2-3 cycles) to confirm cyclical pattern
- **Thorough breast examination**: Assess for lumps, skin changes, nipple discharge, axillary nodes
- **Age-appropriate imaging**:
  - **<40 years with normal examination**: Usually no imaging required (clinical diagnosis)
  - **≥40 years or abnormal examination**: Mammography (± ultrasound)
- **Pregnancy test** if reproductive age and sexually active (exclude pregnancy-related breast changes)

### Second-line Investigations
- **Ultrasound**: If palpable lump or asymmetric nodularity, or in women <40 years (dense breast tissue)
- **Reassessment after menstruation**: Many "lumps" resolve—reexamine in follicular phase (day 7-10 of cycle)
- **Review medications**: OCP, HRT, psychotropic drugs (SSRIs, antipsychotics—can cause hyperprolactinemia)

### Specialist Tests
- **Triple assessment** if concerning features:
  - Clinical examination
  - Imaging (mammography ± ultrasound)
  - Biopsy (fine needle aspiration or core biopsy) if suspicious lesion
- **Prolactin levels**: Only if galactorrhea present or suspected hyperprolactinemia
- **Thyroid function tests**: If other symptoms of thyroid dysfunction
- **MRI breast**: Reserved for high-risk patients or problem-solving (not routine for mastalgia)

## 4. DIAGNOSIS

### Diagnostic Criteria or Clinical Decision Rules
Diagnosis is **clinical**:
- Breast pain with clear **cyclical pattern** (worsens luteal phase, improves with menses)
- Confirmed by **pain diary** over 2-3 cycles
- **Normal breast examination** (or only diffuse nodularity—no discrete mass)
- **Normal imaging** (if performed)
- **Absence of red flag features**

No specific diagnostic test—diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out pathology.

### Key Differential Diagnoses to Exclude
- **Breast cancer** (discrete lump, skin changes, unilateral, non-cyclical, postmenopausal)
- **Breast abscess/mastitis** (erythema, warmth, fever, lactating or recent trauma)
- **Fat necrosis** (history of trauma, firm irregular mass, skin tethering)
- **Fibroadenoma** (discrete, mobile, smooth, well-defined lump—benign but requires assessment)
- **Breast cyst** (discrete, smooth, fluctuant lump; confirmed on ultrasound)
- **Non-cyclical mastalgia** (persistent pain unrelated to cycle—may be musculoskeletal, referred, or idiopathic)
- **Costochondritis/Tietze syndrome** (chest wall pain, tender costochondral junctions, reproducible with palpation)
- **Referred pain**: Cervical spine, thoracic spine, cardiac (angina), gallbladder
- **Pregnancy/lactation-related changes**
- **Medication-induced**: OCP, HRT, SSRIs, methyldopa, spironolactone

## 5. MANAGEMENT

### Acute Management (Emergency/Immediate Care)

Cyclical mastalgia is a **benign, non-urgent condition**. Management is stepwise, starting with reassurance.

#### First-line Treatments
- **Reassurance**: Most important intervention—explain benign nature, no cancer link, often self-limiting
- **Pain diary**: Document pattern to confirm cyclical nature and assess treatment response
- **Supportive, well-fitted bra**: Professional fitting (especially for large breasts); wear during day and night if helpful
- **Simple analgesia**: Paracetamol or NSAIDs (ibuprofen 400 mg TDS) during symptomatic phase
- **Lifestyle modifications**:
  - Reduce caffeine intake (coffee, tea, cola, chocolate)
  - Low-fat, high-complex-carbohydrate diet
  - Regular exercise
  - Stress reduction techniques
- **Dietary supplements** (evidence limited but low risk):
  - **Evening primrose oil** (EPO): 1-3 g daily (contains gamma-linolenic acid); trial for 3-4 months. Not recommended by NICE due to limited evidence, but widely used
  - **Vitamin E**: 400-800 IU daily (limited evidence)
  - Vitamin B6: 50-100 mg daily (limited evidence)

#### Second-line Treatments (if first-line fails after 3-4 months)
- **Topical NSAIDs**: Diclofenac gel or ibuprofen gel applied to affected area TDS (reduces systemic side effects)
- **Modify hormonal contraception**:
  - Stop OCP for trial period (use barrier methods)
  - Or switch to different formulation (lower estrogen, different progestogen)
  - Consider progestogen-only pill or non-hormonal contraception

#### Emergency Procedures
None—cyclical mastalgia is not an emergency. Refer urgently if red flags present (see Red Flags section).

### Chronic Management (Ongoing Care)

#### First-line Treatments
- **Continue lifestyle measures** and well-fitted bra
- **Analgesia as needed** during symptomatic phase
- Most women (80%) respond to reassurance and conservative measures alone

#### Second-line Treatments (Specialist/Breast Clinic)
For **severe, refractory mastalgia** unresponsive to conservative measures:
- **Tamoxifen** (10-20 mg daily during luteal phase or continuously):
  - Selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM)
  - Effective in 70-90% of cases
  - Short-term use (3-6 months) under specialist supervision
  - Side effects: hot flushes, vaginal dryness, menstrual irregularities, thromboembolism risk
  - Contraception essential (teratogenic)
- **Danazol** (100-200 mg daily):
  - Synthetic androgen; suppresses ovulation
  - Effective but significant side effects (androgenic: acne, hirsutism, weight gain, voice deepening, menstrual disturbance)
  - Reserved for severe cases; short-term use only
  - Contraception essential (virilization of female fetus)
- **GnRH analogues** (goserelin):
  - Rarely used due to cost and side effects (menopausal symptoms, bone loss)
  - Reserved for extremely severe cases unresponsive to all other treatments

#### Monitoring Requirements
- **Reassess after 3-4 months** of conservative management
- **Pain diary review** to assess treatment response
- If on tamoxifen/danazol: monitor for side effects, thromboembolism risk
- **Routine breast screening** as per national guidelines (not affected by mastalgia diagnosis)

## 6. DRUGS & PROCEDURES

### Drugs

#### Paracetamol
- **Mechanism of Action**: Central analgesic and antipyretic; inhibits prostaglandin synthesis in CNS
- **Typical Dosing Range**: 500-1000 mg every 4-6 hours (max 4 g/24h)
- **Key Side Effects/Contraindications**: Very safe; hepatotoxicity in overdose; caution in hepatic impairment
- **When to Use vs. Alternatives**: First-line simple analgesia; safe, well-tolerated

#### Ibuprofen (NSAIDs)
- **Mechanism of Action**: Non-selective COX inhibitor; reduces prostaglandin synthesis, anti-inflammatory
- **Typical Dosing Range**: 400 mg TDS with food (max 2.4 g/24h)
- **Key Side Effects/Contraindications**: GI upset, peptic ulceration, renal impairment, cardiovascular risk with long-term use; avoid in asthma, peptic ulcer disease, renal failure
- **When to Use vs. Alternatives**: Effective for inflammatory pain; topical formulations reduce systemic side effects

#### Topical NSAIDs (Diclofenac gel/Ibuprofen gel)
- **Mechanism of Action**: Local anti-inflammatory action; minimal systemic absorption
- **Typical Dosing Range**: Apply to affected area TDS-QDS
- **Key Side Effects/Contraindications**: Local skin irritation; minimal systemic effects
- **When to Use vs. Alternatives**: Preferred over oral NSAIDs for localized pain; safer in elderly, renal impairment

#### Evening Primrose Oil (EPO)
- **Mechanism of Action**: Contains gamma-linolenic acid (GLA)—essential fatty acid precursor to anti-inflammatory prostaglandins; may reduce breast tissue sensitivity to hormones
- **Typical Dosing Range**: 1000-3000 mg daily for 3-4 months
- **Key Side Effects/Contraindications**: Generally safe; nausea, headache (rare); avoid in epilepsy (theoretical seizure risk)
- **When to Use vs. Alternatives**: Not recommended by NICE (limited evidence) but widely used; low risk; trial for 3-4 months

#### Tamoxifen (Specialist use only)
- **Mechanism of Action**: Selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM); blocks estrogen effects on breast tissue
- **Typical Dosing Range**: 10-20 mg daily (luteal phase or continuously) for 3-6 months
- **Key Side Effects/Contraindications**: Hot flushes, vaginal dryness, menstrual irregularity, thromboembolism, endometrial hyperplasia (long-term use); contraindicated in pregnancy/breastfeeding
- **When to Use vs. Alternatives**: Effective (70-90%) but significant side effects; reserve for severe, refractory cases under specialist supervision; requires contraception

#### Danazol (Specialist use only)
- **Mechanism of Action**: Synthetic androgen; suppresses gonadotropins, inhibits ovulation, reduces estrogen production
- **Typical Dosing Range**: 100-200 mg daily for 3-6 months
- **Key Side Effects/Contraindications**: Androgenic effects (acne, hirsutism, weight gain, voice deepening, menstrual disturbance), hepatotoxicity; contraindicated in pregnancy (virilization of fetus)
- **When to Use vs. Alternatives**: Effective but poorly tolerated; use lowest dose for shortest duration; requires contraception

### Procedures

#### Breast biopsy (core biopsy or fine needle aspiration)
- **What it Involves**: Sampling breast tissue for histological/cytological analysis under local anesthesia, usually ultrasound-guided
- **Indications**: Suspicious lump or imaging abnormality requiring tissue diagnosis (NOT routine for cyclical mastalgia)
- **Key Risks/Complications**: Bruising, bleeding, infection, pneumothorax (rare), false negative (sampling error)

## 7. PROGNOSIS & COMPLICATIONS

### Expected Outcomes
- **Benign condition**: No cancer risk associated with cyclical mastalgia
- **Self-limiting in many cases**: 20-30% resolve spontaneously within 3 months; 60% improve with reassurance and conservative measures
- **Recurrence common**: 60% experience recurrent symptoms, but often milder
- **Improves with menopause**: Symptoms typically resolve after menopause (unless on HRT)
- Quality of life impact varies—severe cases may affect sleep, work, relationships

### Important Complications to Watch For
- **No serious medical complications** from cyclical mastalgia itself
- **Psychological impact**: Anxiety about breast cancer (address with reassurance and education)
- **Medication side effects**: If treated with tamoxifen/danazol (thromboembolism, androgenic effects)
- **Overinvestigation**: Unnecessary biopsies if not carefully assessed
- **Missed malignancy**: Always exclude red flags before diagnosing benign cyclical mastalgia

## 8. FOUNDATION DOCTOR ROLE

### Specific Responsibilities and Limitations
Foundation doctors should:
- **Take detailed history**: Pain pattern (cyclical vs. non-cyclical), duration, severity, associated symptoms
- **Perform thorough breast examination**: Check for lumps, skin changes, nipple discharge, axillary nodes
- **Identify red flags**: Discrete lump, skin changes, unilateral bloody discharge, axillary lymphadenopathy
- **Provide reassurance**: Explain benign nature, no cancer link
- **Initiate first-line management**: Pain diary, well-fitted bra, simple analgesia, lifestyle advice
- **Arrange age-appropriate imaging** if indicated (≥40 years or abnormal examination)
- **Refer appropriately**: 2-week wait if red flags; routine breast clinic if severe/refractory
- **Document clearly**: Examination findings, red flags excluded, patient counseled

### When to Escalate to Senior/Specialist
- **Immediate/urgent referral (2-week wait)**:
  - Discrete lump in woman ≥30 years
  - Unilateral bloody nipple discharge
  - Skin changes (peau d'orange, ulceration, nipple retraction)
  - Axillary lymphadenopathy
  - Unilateral pain in postmenopausal woman with no obvious cause
- **Routine breast clinic referral**:
  - Severe mastalgia unresponsive to conservative measures after 3-4 months
  - Patient requesting specialist assessment despite reassurance
  - Diagnostic uncertainty (unable to confirm cyclical pattern, examination equivocal)
  - Discrete lump in woman <30 years (non-urgent referral)
- **No referral needed**:
  - Typical cyclical mastalgia, normal examination, <40 years, responding to conservative measures

### Key Safety Considerations
- **Do not dismiss breast pain**: Always examine and exclude red flags—~5% of breast cancers present with pain
- **Age-appropriate imaging**: Mammography ≥40 years; ultrasound for younger women with abnormal examination
- **Document examination thoroughly**: "No discrete lump, no skin changes, no nipple discharge, no axillary lymphadenopathy" (medicolegal protection)
- **Avoid false reassurance**: Do not say "it's nothing" without proper assessment
- **Safety-netting**: Advise patient to return if:
  - New lump develops
  - Pain becomes persistent/non-cyclical
  - Nipple discharge or skin changes occur
  - Pain worsens or does not respond to treatment
- **Contraception advice**: If prescribing tamoxifen/danazol (teratogenic)
- **Patient education**: Breast self-awareness (not formal self-examination), participation in national screening when eligible
